questions.text:
The graph below shows the average monthly household water usage across New Zealand from 2014 to 2023, with a forecast extending to 2030.

The forecast predicts average monthly water usage will increase significantly by 2030. Evaluate whether this forecast is valid. Support your evaluation with calculations and evidence from the graph.
questions.expectedAnswer: Forecast rate ≈ 21.4 L/year. Historical growth was ≈ 7.8 L/year (2014–2023), so the forecast rate is nearly 3× the historical rate and appears unrealistically high.
questions.markingGuide:
Step 1: Valid evaluation should include: Forecast growth = (900 – 750) ÷ 7 = 21.43 litres/year.

Step 2: Historical: 2014–2023 grew from 680 to 750 (70 litres over 9 years ≈ 7.78 litres/year).

Step 3: The forecast rate is nearly 3× the historical rate — likely too optimistic.

Step 4: Possible reasons the forecast could still be reasonable: population growth, hotter summers increasing garden irrigation, or new appliances.

Step 5: Achieved = describes trend.

Step 6: Merit = justifies with numerical evidence comparing forecast and historical rates.

Final answer: Forecast rate ≈ 21.4 L/year. Historical growth was ≈ 7.8 L/year (2014–2023), so the forecast rate is nearly 3× the historical rate and appears unrealistically high..

questions.text:
Two water providers offer different plans, shown in the table below.

Identify advantages and disadvantages of each provider's plans.
questions.expectedAnswer: AquaSave: cheaper at every tier, carry-over of unused allowance, can share within household. PureFlow: higher litre allowances per tier, free annual hot water check.
questions.markingGuide:
Step 1: AquaSave advantages: Cheaper at every tier (Basic $95 vs $110, Standard $130 vs $145, Unlimited $175 vs $190).

Step 2: Unused allowance carries over.

Step 3: Can share within household.

Step 4: Disadvantages: Lower litres allowance per tier (Basic 15,000 vs 18,000;.

Step 5: Standard 25,000 vs 30,000).

Step 6: PureFlow advantages: Higher litre allowances (Basic 18,000 L vs 15,000 L;.

Step 7: Standard 30,000 L vs 25,000 L).

Step 8: Free annual hot water check on Unlimited.

Step 9: Disadvantages: More expensive at every tier.

Step 10: No carry-over or sharing.

Step 11: Achieved = one advantage from each.

Step 12: Merit = two advantages each.

Step 13: Excellence = comprehensive comparison using numbers from the table.

Final answer: AquaSave: cheaper at every tier, carry-over of unused allowance, can share within household. PureFlow: higher litre allowances per tier, free annual hot water check..

questions.text:
The Tupou family is moving to NZ from Samoa. There are two parents and three children. In Samoa they used about 20,000 L/month. They want a plan that covers their usage and allows garden irrigation.

Recommend either an AquaSave or PureFlow plan. Provide clear reasoning. State any assumptions.
questions.expectedAnswer: AquaSave Standard ($130/mo, 25,000 L) covers 20,000 L current usage with some buffer; AquaSave Unlimited ($175/mo) is safer if garden irrigation significantly raises usage.
questions.markingGuide:
Step 1: Family of 5 currently uses 20,000 L/mo.

Step 2: AquaSave Basic (15,000 L) is not enough.

Step 3: AquaSave Standard ($130, 25,000 L) covers current usage with a 5,000 L buffer.

Step 4: PureFlow Standard ($145, 30,000 L) gives more room but costs $15/mo more.

Step 5: If garden irrigation is significant, an Unlimited plan (AquaSave $175 or PureFlow $190) may be safer.

Step 6: Assumptions to state: whether garden irrigation is a major monthly draw;.

Step 7: whether carry-over and sharing matter;.

Step 8: climate change (Samoa vs NZ) may reduce or increase usage.

Step 9: Achieved = recommendation with one reason.

Step 10: Merit = reasoning on usage AND cost using numbers from the table.

Step 11: Excellence = comprehensive recommendation with assumptions and numerical comparison of at least two plans.

Final answer: AquaSave Standard ($130/mo, 25,000 L) covers 20,000 L current usage with some buffer; AquaSave Unlimited ($175/mo) is safer if garden irrigation significantly raises usage..

questions.text:
The scatter plot below shows the relationship between weekly grocery spending ($) and weekly exercise time (minutes) for different NZ suburbs.

A claim is made that "spending more on groceries means people exercise less." Evaluate this claim using the data in the scatter plot.
questions.expectedAnswer: Moderate negative trend — higher grocery spending tends to correspond with less exercise time, but there is wide spread
questions.markingGuide:
Step 1: The scatter plot shows a moderate negative trend — suburbs with higher grocery spending tend to have lower exercise times.

Step 2: This partially supports the claim.

Step 3: However, there is wide vertical spread at each spending level.

Step 4: Other factors (suburb demographics, access to facilities) also matter.

Step 5: Correlation does not prove causation.

Step 6: Achieved = uses negative trend.

Step 7: Merit = describes strength and discusses limitations.

Final answer: Moderate negative trend — higher grocery spending tends to correspond with less exercise time, but there is wide spread.

Compare features of the grocery spending data. Discuss at least TWO features.
questions.expectedAnswer: Large range ($135), Auckland highest ($280), Gisborne lowest ($145), distribution appears right-skewed
questions.markingGuide:
Step 1: Features: Range is large (280 - 145 = $135/week).

Step 2: Auckland ($280) is highest and pulls the mean up.

Step 3: Distribution is right-skewed (more regions are below the average).

Step 4: Gap between top 3 regions and the rest.

Step 5: Achieved = one feature.

Step 6: Merit = two features with evidence.

Final answer: Large range ($135), Auckland highest ($280), Gisborne lowest ($145), distribution appears right-skewed.

questions.text:
The table below compares grocery-related data for New Zealand and Australia.

NZ has faster-rising grocery costs than Australia. Using the data, identify and explain factors that could account for this. Support with numerical evidence.
questions.expectedAnswer: NZ grocery costs rose 18% vs Australia 12%. NZ smaller population (5.1M vs 26M) may mean less competition and more volatile prices.
questions.markingGuide:
Step 1: Key factors: (1) NZ grocery costs rose 18% vs Australia 12% — a 6 percentage point difference.

Step 2: (2) NZ has 5.1M people vs 26M — smaller market may mean less competition and higher transport costs.

Step 3: (3) Similar organic buying rates (35.5% vs 34%) suggest similar consumer preferences, so the difference is likely supply-side.

Step 4: Achieved = one factor.

Step 5: Merit = one factor with numbers.

Step 6: Excellence = two+ factors with evidence.

Final answer: NZ grocery costs rose 18% vs Australia 12%. NZ smaller population (5.1M vs 26M) may mean less competition and more volatile prices..
